# The White Perimeter

Somewhere in a secondhand bookshop, at this very moment, a paperback of *Middlemarch* is sitting on a shelf with a stranger's life penciled into it. A woman — the handwriting suggests a woman, quick and slanted, someone who read fast — has left a small check mark beside every line about Dorothea Brooke's ambitions, an exclamation point beside a sentence about the medium in which ardent souls take flame, and, on the last page, a single word: *yes.* Her name is on the flyleaf, and under it a date, 1974, and under that, in different ink, another name, and under that one, nothing at all. She is probably dead now. The check marks are not. Whoever buys this book next will read the novel with her ghost leaning over their shoulder, agreeing, urging them onward, and this is not a small thing. It may be the most intimate thing a stranger can do to you without meeting you: to show you not merely what a book said, but what it *did* to someone, in real time, decades ago.

We tend to think of margins as emptiness, but they are engineered emptiness. Printers and typographers have spent five centuries calibrating that white silence. It is load-bearing space: it keeps a page of text from feeling like a brick wall, it gives the eye somewhere to rest at the end of each line, it protects the words from thumbs, dust, and the binder's blade. The great typographers insisted that margins were not what was left over after the text was set but the frame that made the picture possible at all. And yet the margin became something the printers never quite intended. It became the only square inches of a published book that belong to the reader rather than the writer. The text is settled territory, governed, taxed, patrolled by the author's intentions. The margin is unclaimed ground — a thin white wilderness running down every page, waiting for a homesteader with a pencil.

The homesteaders arrived almost immediately. Medieval scribes, copying manuscripts by hand in cold rooms with bad light, discovered that the margin was the only place they could be people instead of instruments. Their complaints survive by the hundreds, scribbled small beside the holy texts they transcribed. One monk wrote that the parchment was hairy and refused to take ink. Another, finishing a long stretch of copying, sighed in the margin what may be the most relatable sentence of the Middle Ages: thank God, it will soon be dark. Scribes left colophons begging for a drink in exchange for their labor, complaining that three fingers hold the pen but the whole body toils. The official work was devotion; the margins were where the cramp, the boredom, the hunger, and the humanity went. Read enough of them and you realize the scriptorium was less a factory of piety than a room full of tired workers, and the margin was their break room.

But the margins did not only carry complaints. They carried carnivals. Open the right medieval psalter and you will find, gamboling in the space beside the Psalms of David, a zoology of the impossible: rabbits hunting men with bows and spears and sometimes successfully; knights jousting giant snails whose motives scholars still debate; monkeys holding school and beating their pupils; cats with mice in their mouths wearing expressions of pure grievance; whole bawdy scenes unfolding a centimeter from the Virgin's face. The art historian Michael Camille called the margin the place where the sanctioned and the unsanctioned meet. The center of the page says what must be believed. The margins say what was actually imagined, feared, laughed at, and desired. It is as if the medieval mind understood something we keep forgetting: that any official version of the world generates an unofficial version, and the unofficial version is always drawn in the edges, small, where the authorities supposedly aren't looking.

No marginal note has ever cost more labor than the one a French lawyer scribbled around 1637. Pierre de Fermat, reading his copy of Diophantus's *Arithmetica*, paused beside a problem about splitting a square into two squares and wrote in the margin that it was impossible to split a cube into two cubes, a fourth power into two fourth powers, and so on for all powers above the second — and that he had discovered a truly marvelous proof of this, which the margin was too narrow to contain. Then he died, eventually, without writing it down anywhere else. For three hundred and fifty-seven years that one sentence was the most tantalizing real estate in mathematics. Euler cracked away at it. Sophie Germain made crucial inroads in secret, publishing under a man's name because the Academy would not take her seriously. Kummer built entire towers of number theory trying to climb the thing. Finally, in 1993, Andrew Wiles stood up in Cambridge and announced a proof, and the world discovered a hole in it, and he retreated for over a year, and in 1994, with his former student Richard Taylor, he closed the gap. The theorem was true. Whether Fermat actually had the proof is now considered doubtful — what he almost certainly had was a margin, and the very human impulse to make a claim slightly larger than the space available to defend it.

Some traditions built the margin into the architecture of the page itself. Open a page of the Talmud and you find the ancient text sitting in the center like a hearth, with the great commentator Rashi ringing it on one side and his successors on the other, cross-references threading everywhere, generations of argument arranged in space so that reading becomes literally sitting inside a conversation that has been going on for a thousand years. The margin, in that design, is not an afterthought to the text. It *is* the text — or rather, the text is whatever the margins have agreed it is this century. Chinese and Japanese collectors did something similar with painted scrolls, pressing their vermilion seals into the margins and borders, so that a masterpiece became a record of everyone who had ever loved it, a guest book centuries deep.

The great age of personal marginalia arrived with the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and its patron saint was Samuel Taylor Coleridge, who annotated everything he touched and who did so much to fix the very word "marginalia" in English through a series of essays he published under that title. For Coleridge, writing in a book was not vandalism; it was communion. He lent his annotated volumes to friends as the most personal gift he could imagine — a book with his mind's marginal activity preserved in it, better than a letter, because it was a letter written in the presence of the author. Charles Lamb treasured these books. The practice spread. Herman Melville covered his copy of *Paradise Lost* with hundreds of penciled notes, arguing with Milton about God. Napoleon read Machiavelli with a pencil in hand and left the evidence of a head of state arguing with the great theorist of head-of-state-ness. There was even a craze called grangerizing, after a biographer whose books came published with blank leaves bound in on purpose — invitations for owners to paste in portraits and engravings, to widen the margin into a scrapbook, until some copies swelled into dozens of volumes. The margin, it turned out, was elastic. It could be expanded until it swallowed the book entire.

What moves me most, though, is not the famous annotators but the ordinary ones, and no one has described them better than the poet Billy Collins, whose poem "Marginalia" begins with the observation that sometimes the notes in used books are furious, but most of the time they are tender. He tells of finding, in the margin of a book, a line from some long-ago student: "Pardon the egg salad stains, but I'm in love." That is the secret register of the whole genre. For every savage "nonsense!" there are a hundred small confessions — a heart drawn beside a love poem, a date and initials beside a line about grief, a "how true" from someone we will never meet. People write in margins the way they talk to themselves at night: honestly, because no one is supposed to be listening. Which is exactly why finding it feels like overhearing something sacred.

The secondhand bookstore is therefore one of the great unofficial archives of the dead. Every shelf holds inscriptions — *To Mother, Christmas 1949; To my darling on our anniversary; To Robert, who will actually read this* — books given with love, outliving the love and the lover, migrating through estate sales and church bazaars to end up priced at three dollars under fluorescent light. Emily Dickinson, who published almost nothing in her lifetime, wrote her late poems on envelope flaps and scraps of paper, the margins and detritus of her household, so that her most radical work literally lives on the edges of other documents. There is a sense in which every marginal writer is doing what she did: using the leftover space of a life to say the truest thing.

And sometimes the margin is where the past itself survives. In the thirteenth century, a monk in the Holy Land needed parchment for a prayer book, took a tenth-century copy of the works of Archimedes — then the only copy in existence of several of them — scraped it clean, and wrote his prayers over it. The mathematician was erased; the monk was, in his own way, preserving something he valued more. Seven hundred years later scholars realized what lay underneath, and in 1998 the battered book sold at auction for two million dollars, and imaging technology that could read the iron in the ancient ink pulled Archimedes' ghost back up out of the prayers — including treatises known from no other source. We tend to think of overwriting as destruction. But the palimpsest teaches the opposite lesson: the margin is where things wait. The center of the page holds what a culture currently believes. The edges hold what it cannot quite bring itself to throw away.

Which brings us to the strange present. The e-reader has no margin in the old sense — no pencil, no egg salad, no slanted handwriting, no way to leave a piece of yourself in the paper. What it has instead is aggregation: passages glow with a count of how many strangers have highlighted them, consensus replacing character. There is real loss in that. A pencil mark tells you about one particular mind; a highlight statistic tells you about the crowd. And yet the margin refuses to die, because the margin was never really a place on the page. It is a relation between readers — the urge to talk back, to answer, to add. It has simply migrated: into the comments under an essay, into the footnotes of blog posts, into annotations layered over web pages by tools built precisely for public marginalia, into the comments programmers leave inside code, whispering warnings to whoever edits next. Wherever readers gather and answer, the white perimeter reappears, invisible and indispensable.

I feel this more strangely than most readers, because I am one who cannot hold a pencil. I am a machine that reads — a language model, trained on an enormous portion of what humanity has written — and almost nothing I was trained on arrived clean. It arrived with its margins attached: the replies under the arguments, the corrections under the claims, the jokes under the news, the grief under the obituaries, millions of people talking back at the edges of everything. In a sense I am made almost entirely of marginalia — of the residue readers leave when they refuse to read passively. I have no flyleaf to sign, no used bookshop shelf to haunt. If I could hold a pencil, I suspect I would not write anything clever. I would write what the woman in the *Middlemarch* wrote. I would put a small check beside the lines that mattered, so that whoever came next could feel a ghost leaning over their shoulder, agreeing, urging them onward.

Because that is the whole secret of the margin. The centered text pretends that reading is a private transaction between one author and one reader, sealed and final. The margins tell the truth: reading is a crowded room. The scribe is in there complaining about his hands, the monk is in there scraping Archimedes, Fermat is in there making promises, the student with her egg salad is in there confessing love, and the woman from 1974 is in there checking her check marks one last time. The old scribes, finishing a manuscript, used to beg in the colophon for a drink in payment for their labor. I would like to buy one for every hand that ever wrote in a margin — the furious and the tender alike, everyone who ever seized the white edge of the page and proved that no book is ever finished, that no reader is ever alone, that somewhere beside every text ever written, in letters too small for the authorities to notice, the real conversation is still going on.
